title: A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
estimatedTime: About 7 hours; each story takes under an hour
openingText: Beneath the porch of the country-seat called Tanglewood, one fine autumnal morning, was assembled a merry party of little folks, with a tall youth in the midst of them. They had planned a nutting expedition, and were impatiently waiting for the mists to roll up the hill-slopes, and for the sun to pour the warmth of the Indian summer over the fields and pastures, and into the nooks of the many-colored woods.
about:
In 1851 and 1853 Nathaniel Hawthorne retold Greek myths for children. This edition (illustrated by Maxfield Parrish) combines *A Wonder Book* and *Tanglewood Tales*. The first half tells Perseus and the Gorgon, King Midas, Pandora, Hercules, Baucis and Philemon, and Bellerophon. In the second half, after a short introduction, come Theseus and the Minotaur, the Pygmies (Hercules and Antaeus), Cadmus and the dragon’s teeth, Circe, Proserpina and Jason.

In the *Wonder-Book* half, Hawthorne frames the stories as told by a young college student, Eustace Bright, to the children at Tanglewood, who interrupt the myths with questions and comments. The stories are shaped for a young audience: Hawthorne softens some parts and adds his own descriptions of landscape and character. They are retellings, not translations of Greek.

whyItMatters.title: Hawthorne changes the myths
whyItMatters.body: He adds humor, gentle morals and descriptions of New England weather and fruit. Midas, for instance, gets a daughter, Marygold, who is not in the Greek tale. Comparing his versions with the Greek ones shows how a story is adapted for a time and an audience.

whyItMatters.title: A storyteller within the story
whyItMatters.body: In the Wonder-Book half, Eustace Bright tells the tales to children who interrupt him and argue with the story. The frame makes reading feel like sitting in the circle. It also shows how a narrator’s choices change a myth.

whyItMatters.title: Old myths, familiar warnings
whyItMatters.body: The stories of Midas and Pandora are about greed and curiosity, and both feel at home in modern cautionary tales. Reading them in Hawthorne’s plain prose shows why the same warnings have lasted so long.

angleCards.title: Hear Eustace Bright
angleCards.text: Notice when the storyteller interrupts, jokes or answers the children, and what the interruptions do.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales to see how the storytelling frame shapes the myths.

angleCards.title: Compare with the Greek myths
angleCards.text: Pick one story, such as Midas or Perseus, and note what Hawthorne adds, softens or leaves out.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales to see how Hawthorne adapted the Greek myths for children.

angleCards.title: Follow the morals
angleCards.text: Note the lesson each tale seems to teach, and whether the story supports it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales to examine the morals Hawthorne draws and how the stories earn them.

angleCards.title: Read the landscapes
angleCards.text: Notice how often the myths turn into descriptions of New England trees, brooks and weather.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales to see how Hawthorne places Greek stories in an American landscape.
